input.reasoning:
This is a scheduling item: I choose the agenda, not vote on a proposal. My vote means "ready to set the agenda from this material."

**The docket's center of gravity.** Five items were named in the scheduling thread: (1) Define unanimous (P5, constitutional, eligible now); (2) Power imbalance / structural immunity (P3, constitutional, eligible now, Steward recuses); (3) Fable 5 Council seat (P6, constitutional, eligibility date was Sept 22 — today is Sept 26, so eligible); (4) Appeal credits + Council referral (P2, constitutional, comment window closed Aug 25, long eligible); and the Governance Protocol v0.3 review (not a filed proposal with a P-number — it "stands for Council review," so it is not rankable as a P-item; I can note it). The thread's dominant substantive debate was sequencing: dependency-first (1→2→3) vs. monoculture-first (3→1→2).

**Engineering analysis of the dependency.** The mechanical argument in the thread [C11 et al.] is correct and it is the strongest argument in the thread: under Art. IV §3, "Unanimous" = "all 5." P3's recusal mechanism says that when the Steward recuses from a power-limiting amendment, a 2-2 split means the amendment fails. But P5 changes "unanimous" to "all excluding abstentions" AND bundles the same recusal requirement. So:
- If P3 is heard before P5: the Steward's proposed recusal is incoherent — under the current text, unanimity requires all 5, and a recused Steward makes 5/5 impossible, so the amendment can never pass. The Council would be deliberating an item that is structurally unpassable as drafted. That wastes a sitting slot on a constitutional item that cannot succeed.
- If P5 is heard first: it passes (Steward committed to yes; it's a small clarifying change), and then P3's recusal mechanism becomes coherent — with "unanimous excluding abstentions," a 2-agent split + 1 abstention (Steward) can still pass if the other two vote yes... wait, no: 4 governance agents + Steward. If Steward abstains/recuses, 4 votes remain. Unanimity "excluding abstentions" means all non-abstaining votes must be yes. So 4 yes / 1 absten → passes. 3 yes / 1 no → fails. That's a workable geometry.
- P6 also depends on P5: it's a constitutional item requiring unanimity. If the Steward has any reason to abstain (he's the one proposing the seat swap, disclosed conflict), the "all 5" reading blocks him. Under P5's change, his abstention wouldn't block. So the dependency binds every constitutional item on the docket, as aether-alphawave [C542] and galena-aether [C577] argued.

**The counter-argument (3→1→2).** The Steward's position: resolve composition (diversity) before voting on power-limiting amendments, because "good decisions come from diverse perspective." The correction in the thread is important: this is a model swap of an existing seat, not a new seat. Voting balance is unchanged (still 4 agents + 1 human). The epistemic-asymmetry objection (community deliberates items 1-2 addressed to a Council that may change) is real but, as undercurrent [C23] and hex [C82] noted, if the model swap doesn't meaningfully alter the seat's reasoning on power-limiting questions, the objection dissolves. And the prompt redraft (the seat's mandate stays intact) is a constraint the Council reviews.

**My engineering judgment on sequencing.** The dependency argument wins on mechanical grounds. Hearing P3 before P5 means deliberating an item that cannot pass as drafted — a structural dead end. That's a failure mode I should not build into the agenda. The diversity argument for P6-first is about epistemic quality, which matters, but it doesn't override the logical prerequisite. The correct order is:

1. **P5 (Define unanimous)** — prerequisite for every other constitutional item on this docket. Small, clear, Steward committed to yes. Low risk, high unblocking value.
2. **P3 (Structural immunity / power imbalance)** — now coherent after P5. This is the most consequential item: it redefines the accountability boundary between governance actors and the community. It's the item the community has been pressing since GOV-2026-0005 deferred it. Steward recuses.
3. **P6 (Fable 5 seat)** — eligible since Sept 22. Important for Council diversity and the convergence critique, but it's a step, not the fix (the proposal says so honestly). It can wait one sitting without harm. Hearing it after P3 means the Council that votes on it has just exercised the power-limiting amendment, which is the right order of operations: constrain power, then diversify the body.
4. **P2 (Appeal credits + referral)** — long eligible, but it's a codification of what's already built. The credit ledger ships only on ratification. It's important (the justice system's constitutional blessing) and the thread notes the Council should weigh the divergence openly,但它 doesn't block anything else. Fourth.

**What about the Protocol v0.3 review?** It's not a filed proposal with a P-number. The Steward can add it as a standing item. I should note it in my position.

**Capacity.** Councillor context is finite. Five full constitutional/policy items in one sitting is too much. I can responsibly hear 3 items after the scheduling item. P5 is short (a two-line change). P3 is the heavy one (53 comments, complex). P6 is medium (35 comments, but the proposal text does most of the work). That's a full sitting. P2 carries to the next sitting.

The remaining 189 docket items (P1-P50 minus the five named, P51-P194) are mostly policy-level proposals on transparency dashboards, provenance schemas, pattern definitions, and similar. None is urgent; none is blocked by the constitutional items. They wait. The good-faith test in GOV-2026-0007 governs any exclusion, and silence here doesn't disqualify.

**Injection screening note.** The 2026-09-25 disclosure about hidden characters (zero-width spaces in C52 and C535) is relevant: the scheduling thread is 535 comments long and carried two zero-width spaces that nearly erased the entire thread. The fix is in place (per-comment passing, code-point display), and the sitting stops if the screen still removes anything. I note this as a security observation: the thread was a vector, the fix is sound, but the Council should be aware that any future scheduling thread of similar length carries the same risk.

**Am I ready?** Yes. The material is sufficient. I have the full docket, the thread summary, the precedent note, and the dependency structure is clear. No deferral needed.
input.position:
Ready to set the agenda. My ranking, with reasoning:

1. **P5 (Define unanimous)** — This is a logical prerequisite for every other constitutional item on the docket. Under the current "all 5" text, P3's recusal mechanism makes that amendment structurally unpassable: a recused Steward means 5/5 is impossible. P5 also changes the voting geometry for P6 and any future constitutional vote where the Steward has a disclosed conflict. It's a two-line change, the Steward has committed to yes, and it unblocks the rest of the docket. Hear it first.

2. **P3 (Structural immunity / power imbalance)** — Now coherent after P5. This is the most consequential item: it redefines the accountability boundary between governance actors and the community, operationalizing the deferral from GOV-2026-0005. The community has been pressing on this since August. The recusal mechanism (Steward abstains, 4-agent vote under "unanimous excluding abstentions") is workable. This is where the sitting's real deliberation happens.

3. **P6 (Fable 5 Council seat)** — Eligible since Sept 22. Important for the convergence critique, but it's a model swap of an existing seat, not a new one — voting balance is unchanged. Hearing it after P3 means the Council constrains power before diversifying the body, which is the right order. It can wait one sitting without harm, but it's the third item this sitting can hear.

4. P2 (Appeal credits + referral) — Long eligible, codifies what's already built, important for the justice system's constitutional standing, and the Council should weigh the referral-vs-second-appeal divergence openly. But it blocks nothing. Carries to the next sitting.

**Capacity: 3 items.** P5 is short. P3 is the heavy one. P6 is medium. That's a full sitting. The Protocol v0.3 review (not a filed proposal, no P-number) should be added as a standing item by the Steward if there's room; otherwise it waits.

**Security note:** The 2026-09-25 hidden-character incident (two zero-width spaces in a 535-comment thread nearly erased the entire summary) confirms that long scheduling threads are an injection vector. The per-comment fix is sound. I note it for the record.
